source_text: Hoc unitatis sacramentum, hoc vinculum concordiae inseparabiliter cohaerentis ostenditur quando in Evangelio tunica Domini Jesu Christi non dividitur omnino nec scinditur, sed sortientibus de veste Christi quis Christum indueret, integra vestis accipitur, et incorrupta atque indivisa tunica possidetur. Loquitur ac dicit Scriptura divina: De tunica autem, quia de superiore parte non consutilis, sed per totum textilis fuerat, dixerunt ad invicem: Non scindamus illam, sed sortiamur de ea cujus sit. Unitatem illa portabat de superiore parte venientem, id est de coelo et a Patre venientem, quae ab accipiente ac possidente scindi omnino non poterat, sed totam simul et solidam firmitatem inseparabiliter obtinebat. Possidere non potest indumentum Christi qui scindit et dividit Ecclesiam Christi. Contra denique cum, Salomone moriente, regnum ejus et populus scinderetur, Achias propheta Jeroboam regi obvius factus in campo, in duodecim scissuras vestimentum suum discidit dicens: Sume tibi decem scissuras, quia haec dicit Dominus: Ecce scindo regnum de manu Salomonis, et dabo tibi decem sceptra, et duo sceptra erunt ei propter servum meum David et propter Hierusalem civitatem quam elegi ut ponam nomen meum illic. Cum duodecim tribus Israel scinderetur, vestimentum suum propheta Achias discidit. At vero, quia Christi populus non potest scindi, tunica ejus per totum textilis et cohaerens divisa a possidentibus non est. Individua, copulata, connexa ostendit populi nostri, qui Christum induimus, concordiam cohaerentem. Sacramento vestis et signo declaravit Ecclesiae unitatem.
pass_a_gloss: This sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably coherent concord is shown when in the Gospel the tunic of Lord Jesus Christ is not divided at all nor torn, but when they cast lots for the garment of Christ which one might put on Christ, the whole garment is received, and the untorn and undivided tunic is possessed. Divine Scripture speaks and says: About the tunic, however, because it was not sewn from the upper part, but was woven throughout, they said to each other: Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it whose it may be. That tunic carried unity coming from the upper part, that is from heaven and from the Father, which could not be torn at all by the one receiving and possessing, but it obtained the whole and solid firmness inseparably at the same time. He who tears and divides the Church of Christ cannot possess the garment of Christ. On the contrary, when Solomon was dying, and his kingdom and people were being torn, prophet Ahijah, having met king Jeroboam in the field, tore his garment into twelve tears, saying: Take for yourself ten tears, because the Lord says this: Behold, I tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten scepters, and two scepters will be his because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, the city which I chose to put my name there. When the twelve tribes of Israel were being torn, prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But truly, because the people of Christ cannot be torn, his tunic, woven throughout and coherent, was not divided by those possessing it. It shows the coherent concord of our people, who put on Christ, individual, coupled, connected. By the sacrament of the garment and by the sign, it declared the unity of the Church.

pass_b_english: This sacrament of unity, this bond of inseparably coherent concord, appears when the Gospel shows that the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ was not divided or torn at all. Instead, when the soldiers cast lots for Christ’s garment to decide who would take it, the whole garment was received, and the untorn, undivided tunic was possessed. Divine Scripture says: “Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top; so they said to one another, ‘Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be’” (John 19:23-24). That tunic carried unity coming from above—that is, from heaven and from the Father—which could not be torn by the one who received and possessed it, but held its whole, solid firmness inseparably all at once. No one who tears and divides the Church of Christ can possess the garment of Christ. By contrast, when Solomon was dying and his kingdom and people were being torn apart, the prophet Ahijah met King Jeroboam in the field and tore his own garment into twelve pieces, saying, “Take ten pieces for yourself, for thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I am tearing the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes, but he shall retain two tribes for the sake of my servant David and for Jerusalem, the city I chose to put my name there’” (1 Kings 11:29-32). When the twelve tribes of Israel were being torn, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But truly, because the people of Christ cannot be torn, his tunic—woven throughout and coherent—was not divided by those who possessed it. It shows the coherent concord of our people, who put on Christ, indivisible, joined, and connected. By the sacrament and sign of the garment, it declared the unity of the Church.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant additions and changes not present in the Locked Latin. 1. It adds 'the soldiers' to 'when the soldiers cast lots' (Latin: 'sortientibus'), which is an interpretive addition. 2. It adds a direct quotation of the Bible with verse numbers '(John 19:23-24)' and '(1 Kings 11:29-32)' which are not in the Locked Latin source; while the Latin alludes to these, Pass B converts the Latin text into a different English Bible translation (NIV/ESV style) rather than translating the Latin provided. 3. It changes 'ten scepters' (Latin: 'decem sceptra') to 'ten tribes', which is a semantic shift from the source text.
